title: Caravels and carracks: the ships of the Age of Discovery
summary: Carracks and caravels were the main ships of the early Age of Discovery. The caravel, a small trading vessel rigged with lateen sails, was used heavily from the 14th to the 17th centuries and made some of the earliest Atlantic crossings. The carrack, a blend of Atlantic and Mediterranean ship types, had room for a large crew and cargo. Columbus's Santa Maria and Magellan's Victoria were carracks, and the Portuguese used carracks in their Indian Ocean trade.

uncertainty.note: The id year 1000 reflects the medieval diffusion of lateen-rigged vessels; The Mariners' Museum dates the carrack to 1200-1600 CE and the caravel to 1400-1600 CE.

where.modern_name: Lisbon, Portugal (stand-in pin for Atlantic ship design and voyages)
where.historical_name: Lisbon, Kingdom of Portugal (hub of caravel and carrack construction and departure point for oceanic expeditions)

importance.justification: These ships made the long ocean voyages of the Age of Discovery possible.

related.because: The technical synthesis of caravel manoeuvrability and carrack cargo capacity provided the vessels required for systematic transoceanic exploration.
Lateen-rigged caravels enabled Portuguese mariners to tack against offshore African winds and round Cape Bojador.
